posts.title: Week 1 — Learning Unreal Through the Backrooms
posts.preview: For my first time using Unreal Engine 5, I moved away from following the tutorial step-by-step and instead explored materials, Blueprints, C++, and procedural maze generation through a simple Backrooms-inspired environment.

content.text: For our first assignment, we were asked to explore a video tutorial introducing us to Unreal Engine. I watched some of it to understand the basics, but I have never really enjoyed learning by following video tutorials step-by-step. I usually understand a tool better when I have something I actually want to make and can figure things out as I go.

So, for my first time using Unreal Engine 5, I decided to build a small Backrooms-inspired environment. I was mainly interested in exploring two things: how to construct an environment in Unreal, and what kinds of scripting and procedural systems I could create inside it. The second part was especially interesting to me because I enjoy working with systems and code.

content.alt: Early Backrooms environment created in Unreal Engine 5
content.caption: An early version of the Backrooms environment.

content.text: Starting with Materials

I started with some very basic Unreal workflows. First, I created a master material that I could use as the base for other materials in the environment. From that, I could quickly create variations instead of rebuilding every material from scratch.

content.alt: M_Backrooms_Master material graph connecting base color, normal, and roughness textures with texture size, tint, and ambient glow parameters
content.caption: The master material: a reusable setup for textures, scale, tint, roughness, and ambient glow.

content.text: This was a useful introduction to the way Unreal organizes materials and parameters. Even in a simple environment like this, having a reusable material system made it much easier to experiment with how the space looked.

For the fluorescent panels, I made a separate, much simpler material. I multiplied a light color by an emissive strength parameter and connected the result to Emissive Color. This gave me controls for the color and intensity of the panel's glow.

content.alt: M_FluorescentPanel material graph multiplying LightColor by EmissiveStrength and connecting the result to Emissive Color
content.caption: The fluorescent panel material, with parameters for light color and emissive strength.

content.alt: Material and environment experimentation in Unreal Engine
content.caption: Experimenting with the visual structure of the environment.

content.text: Building with Blueprints

Next, I started creating Blueprints for the pieces that made up the environment. The Backrooms cell brought together a floor, ceiling, and four walls. Its Construction Script used a boolean for each wall to control visibility and collision, so the same cell could have different openings. I also made a separate Blueprint for the fluorescent panels. This helped me understand how reusable components could be assembled into a larger environment.

content.alt: BP_BackroomsCell Construction Script using branches to toggle visibility and collision for the north, south, east, and west walls
content.caption: The reusable Backrooms cell Blueprint, with controls for which walls are present.

content.alt: Procedurally generated Backrooms maze in Unreal Engine
content.caption: Developing the modular environment and maze structure.

content.text: I initially tried to generate the maze using Blueprint nodes too. I used nested loops to place cells on a grid, a random stream to make wall choices, and spawn nodes for the cells and fluorescent panels. But I couldn't get the generation working the way I wanted. As the graph grew, the wiring became harder for me to follow, and I was spending more time tracing connections than working through the maze logic.

content.alt: Blueprint maze-generation graph with nested grid loops, random wall choices, and nodes for spawning Backrooms cells and fluorescent panels
content.caption: My attempt at generating the maze with Blueprint nodes. I couldn't get this working as intended, which led me to try code.

content.text: Switching to C++

Since I wasn't getting the node-based generator to work, I decided to switch to C++ for the procedural maze generation. Working in code felt much more natural to me: I could describe the rules of the maze directly and follow the logic more easily. The material graphs and reusable environment pieces were still part of the project; it was the generation logic that I moved into code.

Once the maze generation started working, the project became much more interesting. The same relatively small collection of walls, ceilings, floors, and lights could create a space with a surprising amount of variation. It began to feel less like a scene I had manually constructed and more like a system capable of producing different versions of the environment.

content.alt: Final procedural Backrooms environment running in Unreal Engine 5
content.caption: The procedural maze generating a larger Backrooms-like environment.

content.text: What I Learned

There is still a lot I would improve. The textures, lighting, color, and overall mood could all be pushed much further. Working on this made me realize how much an environment depends on these subtle details. It is not necessarily about filling a space with lots of props; small changes in texture, light, repetition, scale, and atmosphere can completely change how the space feels.

For a first experiment in Unreal, though, I liked that I was able to make something relatively simple that still produced an interesting result. More importantly, I got to move through several different parts of the Unreal workflow—materials, Blueprints, reusable environment pieces, and C++ scripting—while building one small project.

Rather than trying to completely understand Unreal before making anything, this felt like a much better way for me to begin learning it: start with an idea, build until I hit a problem, and then learn whatever part of the tool I need in order to solve it.

posts.title: Week 2 — Making the Backrooms Feel Unstable
posts.preview: This week, I developed three conditions for the Backrooms maze: normal, worn, and heavily degraded. Through material experiments, ChatGPT references, an iterative MCP workflow, and a shrine generated in Tripo, I started exploring how the same space could move between an ordinary office and something much more disturbing.

content.text: Last week, I built a basic Backrooms environment and got the procedural maze generation working. This week, I wanted to spend more time on how the space actually felt. I had the structure of a maze, but the rooms needed more variation, and I wanted that variation to become part of the idea behind the game.
Three Versions of the Same Space

The idea is to have three broad types of rooms: normal, slightly messed up, and very messed up. The normal rooms are fairly ordinary office spaces, with repetitive wallpaper, carpet, ceiling panels, and fluorescent lights. The slightly messed-up rooms have stains, scuffed and peeling walls, damaged ceiling panels, and flickering lights. The most extreme rooms push this much further, with gore, bones, hanging intestines, a face emerging from a wall, and a shrine surrounded by candles.

I am interested in how unpredictable the transitions between these conditions can feel. You might walk through a room that seems completely normal, turn a corner into something disturbing, and then find yourself back in an ordinary office corridor. I want that return to normal to feel uncomfortable too. Once you have seen what can exist in this space, it becomes harder to trust a room just because it looks harmless.

This is starting to become my own fictional extension of the Backrooms. Eventually, I want a monster to hunt the player through the maze, but I will get into that part of the concept in the next post. For now, I am working on the environment and the sense of paranoia that can come from moving through it.
Starting with Stains

I started with a fairly simple version of degradation: adding stains and wear to the walls. I wanted to see how much I could change the atmosphere while keeping the basic room recognizable. The first attempt gave me something to react to, but the overall result was looking greenish and dull.

content.alt: First wall-degradation experiment in the Unreal Backrooms environment
content.caption: Degradation attempt 1: starting with stains and basic wear on the walls.

content.alt: Backrooms scene used to check the overall colour and lighting of the early experiment
content.caption: A vibe check of the early result. The colour and lighting still felt dull.

content.text: I tried making a few more adjustments, but I was still not getting the result I wanted. There was visible damage, yet the room as a whole did not feel convincing. This became a recurring part of the process: a change could add more detail without necessarily improving the atmosphere.

content.alt: Follow-up degradation experiment with more visible wall stains and wear
content.caption: Degradation attempt 2.1: more adjustments, but the overall look was still not quite working.

content.text: Finding the Right Colour and Atmosphere

I then looked at an image of the Backrooms from the internet. What stood out to me was the relationship between the surfaces: the floor looked yellower, while the walls had more of a green tint. That gave me a more specific direction for the colour of my own environment. I needed to consider the floor, walls, ceiling, and lighting together.

content.alt: Backrooms reference image with yellow flooring, greenish walls, and fluorescent ceiling lights
content.caption: The internet reference I used to reconsider the colour balance, particularly the yellower floor and greener walls.

content.text: The next few attempts explored different degrees of damage and darkness. I was trying to establish a range of room conditions while keeping them connected to the same underlying space. The material colours, visible wear, and lighting all affected how far a room seemed to have deteriorated.

content.alt: Second degradation experiment in the Unreal editor
content.caption: Degradation attempt 2: continuing to work through the colour and surface treatment.

content.alt: Backrooms room with heavier stains and more extensive surface damage
content.caption: Degradation attempt 3: pushing the room towards a more heavily damaged condition.

content.alt: Darker variation of the degraded Backrooms environment
content.caption: Degradation attempt 3.1: testing how the damaged surfaces read in a darker room.

content.text: Making the References More Specific

At this point, I wanted a clearer visual target for the different rooms. I asked ChatGPT to generate a reference mood board with isometric views of the variations I was imagining. These explored the range from ordinary office rooms to worn spaces and the more extreme horror rooms. Seeing them together helped me think about the differences between the room types.

content.alt: ChatGPT-generated mood board showing isometric concepts for several Backrooms room conditions
content.caption: A ChatGPT-generated reference mood board for the room variations. These are concept images, not screenshots from Unreal.

content.text: I also generated more focused references for the walls and gore. The room views were useful for the overall atmosphere, but I needed closer references to explain what individual details should look like: how wallpaper peels away from a wall, how the gore sits against a surface, and how these elements relate to the rest of the room.

content.alt: ChatGPT-generated concept image for a heavily degraded Backrooms room with gore
content.caption: A generated reference for the appearance and placement of gore in the more extreme rooms.

content.text: Getting the MCP Workflow to Work

A major part of this week's process was setting up the MCP connection and figuring out how to use it to make changes in Unreal. My workflow became a repeated cycle of describing a change, checking the result in the scene, identifying what felt wrong, and revising the instructions. The references gave me something concrete to compare the results against.

The first attempts at peeling wallpaper and gore did not work very well. The peeling wallpaper was especially unconvincing: the shapes on the wall did not read as wallpaper separating from the surface. I had to get more specific about the appearance I wanted and revisit the references.

content.alt: Early MCP-generated peeling-wallpaper attempt with raised shapes on the wall
content.caption: The first peeling-wallpaper result. It needed more work to read as a layer coming away from the wall.

content.text: The gore also needed several passes. One version was much too shiny, which made the material feel wrong even when the general placement was closer to what I wanted. I asked for a more matte appearance and kept refining the forms and surface treatment.

content.alt: An intermediate gore treatment with overly glossy surfaces beneath a fluorescent light
content.caption: An intermediate gore result that was too shiny. The surface appearance was revised in later passes.

content.text: I went back to ChatGPT to create more detailed visual references for the gore and peeling walls. This made the feedback easier to explain. I could point to a particular edge, surface, or shape and use that to guide the next attempt. I also used a separate reference for the face emerging from the wall.

content.alt: ChatGPT-generated detail reference showing peeling wallpaper and gore
content.caption: A more detailed generated reference used to guide another pass on the peeling wallpaper and gore.

content.alt: Reference image of a face appearing to push out through a Backrooms wall
content.caption: The reference for the face emerging from the wall.

content.text: Technically, I was working across several connected parts of the environment: material colour and surface appearance, wall damage, ceiling details, lighting and flicker, and the placement of additional forms and props. The C++ maze from Week 1 provided the procedural structure. This week's work focused on developing the conditions of the rooms within that structure.

Getting the MCP workflow to work for me depended on making the feedback more specific. A broad request to make a room look degraded left a lot open to interpretation. Checking each result and describing the particular thing that needed to change made the process much more useful.
Building the Shrine

For the shrine, I generated an asset in Tripo and brought it into the environment. I have also taken some inspiration from Warhammer 40K and Doom (2016). The shrine and candles belong to the most heavily degraded room. This is where the project starts moving further into its own fiction: something has happened in this space, but I am not explaining what it is yet.

content.alt: Shrine asset generated in Tripo, with candles and dark organic forms around its base
content.caption: The shrine asset I generated in Tripo before bringing it into the environment.

content.text: Walking Through the Current Maze

The following GIFs show the current result. The sequence begins in the well-lit rooms and moves through increasingly damaged spaces before returning to the ordinary maze. Walking through them helped me judge how the different conditions worked together.

content.alt: Walking through the well-lit normal rooms of the procedural Backrooms maze
content.caption: 1. Walking through the well-lit rooms, establishing the ordinary version of the space.

content.alt: Moving into a worn Backrooms room with wall damage, hanging ceiling elements, and flickering lights
content.caption: 2. Moving into a slightly scuffed room, with damaged walls, hanging ceiling elements, and flickering lights.

content.alt: Walking through the dark, ordinary rooms of the connected Backrooms maze
content.caption: 3. Moving through the maze of ordinary rooms, where the similar spaces make it easy to lose your sense of direction.

content.text: The maze is still an important part of the experience. Repeated walls, openings, and turns make it difficult to build a clear picture of the space. The different room conditions give that repetition another layer of uncertainty.

content.alt: Running through several connected rooms in the procedurally generated maze
content.caption: 4. Running through the connected rooms to show the maze layout and the procedural structure of the environment.

content.text: In the most degraded rooms, the environment becomes much more bodily. Gore spreads across the walls and ceiling, with bones and intestines hanging into the space. The face emerging from the wall adds another uncomfortable detail to an otherwise familiar surface.

content.alt: Entering a heavily degraded Backrooms room with gore extending across the ceiling
content.caption: 5. Entering the gore-filled rooms, where the ceiling and walls take on a much more disturbing appearance.

content.alt: A face emerging from the wall beside gore in a heavily degraded Backrooms room
content.caption: 6. The face emerging from the wall, surrounded by the gore in the most degraded room.

content.alt: The first view of the shrine and candles in a dark Backrooms room
content.caption: 7. The first look at the shrine and candles.

content.alt: Moving closer to the shrine and candles in the most heavily degraded Backrooms room
content.caption: 8. Moving closer to the shrine and its candles.

content.alt: Another view of the shrine and candle arrangement in the dark Backrooms room
content.caption: 9. Another view of the shrine and candles.

content.text: The sequence ends by returning to the ordinary office maze. I like this part of the idea because the environment seems to carry on as if nothing has happened. The normal rooms are still there, but they feel different after moving through the others.

content.alt: Running through the normal Backrooms corridors again after visiting the degraded rooms
content.caption: 10. Back to the ordinary liminal space, as if everything is normal again.

content.text: Where I Want to Take This

This week helped me develop a way of working between visual references, the MCP connection, and the scene in Unreal. The results improved through a lot of small corrections. The failed attempts were useful because they made me more precise about what I wanted the next version to do.

I want to keep developing the relationship between the three room conditions and how unexpectedly the player encounters them. The monster is the next part of that exploration, and I will reveal more about its role in the next post. For now, the maze is beginning to feel like a place whose ordinary appearance cannot always be trusted.
